bibliography.title: Expressivity-Efficiency Tradeoffs for Hybrid Sequence Models

sections.title: 3 Function Compositions and Limitations of Pure Models

abstract_sentences.text: Hybrid sequence models—combining Transformer and state-space model layers—seek to gain the expressive versatility of attention as well as the computational efficiency of state-space model layers.
Despite burgeoning interest in hybrid models, we lack a basic understanding of the settings where—and underlying mechanisms through which—they offer benefits over their constituent models.
In this paper, we study this question, focusing on a broad family of core synthetic tasks.
For this family of tasks, we prove the existence of fundamental limitations for non-hybrid models.
Specifically, any Transformer or state-space model that solves the underlying task requires either a large number of parameters or a large working memory.

evidence.anchor: large number of parameters or a large working memory

abstract_sentences.text: On the other hand, for two prototypical tasks within this family—namely selective copying and associative recall—we construct hybrid models of small size and working memory that provably solve these tasks, thus achieving the best of both worlds.

evidence.anchor: hybrid models of small size and working memory

abstract_sentences.text: Our experimental evaluation empirically validates our theoretical findings.
Importantly, going beyond the settings in our theoretical analysis, we empirically show that learned—rather than constructed—hybrids outperform non-hybrid models with up to 6× as many parameters.
We additionally demonstrate that hybrid models exhibit stronger length generalization and out-of-distribution robustness than non-hybrids.

evidence.anchor: stronger length generalization and out-of-distribution robustness

final_judgment.single_storyline: Function-composition tasks split long-context control extraction from local content-addressable retrieval. Conditional lower bounds assign the first bottleneck to sliding-window Transformer windows and the second to SSM state, while SSM-first Hybrid constructions distribute the jobs across layers.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: Definitions, assumptions, theorem statements, Figures 1–8, Table 1, C1–C3, and the p. 12 limitation sentence keep the decision path visible without the appendix.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: C/D contain all proof steps and matrix constructions; D.5 contains construction visualizations; E contains optimizer, repetitions, task settings, and sensitivity scans.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Use one task decomposition to align a resource bound, an explicit construction, learned-model curves, and a scope statement in the same narrative order.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The formal scope is limited to injection/local-sensitivity tasks and sliding-window attention. Evidence remains synthetic, and learned comparisons retain layer-count, parameter-composition, optimization, and Table-1 uncertainty limits.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For a hybrid architecture claim, first isolate two distinct resource bottlenecks in a task, then connect lower bounds, a construction, trained baselines, and distribution-shift checks to the same mechanism.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: Use this rule only when task structure, resource definitions, baseline attention form, and data-distribution assumptions are explicit. It does not by itself explain real-world behavior dominated by optimization, data, or external memory.
